repos.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
repos.paper_summary:
EnvOpt treats the stationary environment (the data, documents, and tools an agent works in) as a third optimization target alongside model parameters and harness. A coding agent acts as a research agent. It runs the target agent on unlabeled training tasks, edits the environment (for example, adding cheatsheets, indexes, databases, or tools), and keeps edits that lower cost. It may not modify the harness. A held-out validation set with verifiers decides when to stop.

On AutomationBench with Claude Haiku 4.5 as target, cost falls 72.7% and pass rate rises 14.3%. The optimized environment transfers to Claude Opus 5, with 68.1% cost reduction and a 1.34% pass-rate gain. On top of Meta-Harness, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across five benchmarks, average cost falls 48% on unseen test tasks, with pass rates improved or maintained.

Limitations: without verifiers, the research agent sometimes used proxies such as answer length, which hurt held-out performance. An early bug also persisted across four later steps. The authors report that three training steps were empirically safe without a validation set but still recommend one.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Environment optimization is proposed as a third axis, alongside parameter tuning and harness optimization, for improving LLM agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: EnvOpt runs a research agent that edits the environment over disjoint training steps, stopping when validation cost rises.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: EnvOpt cuts Haiku 4.5 cost by 72.7% on AutomationBench and raises pass rate by 14.3%, and it transfers to other models.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Successful edits included converters, cheatsheets and databases, while oversized files and over-broad search tools raised cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Environment optimization is presented as a third direction that cuts agent cost while maintaining or improving success across five benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists research agent instructions for AutomationBench, Workspace-Bench, Data-Eng-Bench, Bleve and Tenacity.

repos.title: Householder Motion Embedding: Noise Modulation for Motion-Controllable Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: Householder Motion Embedding (HME) is a noise-initialization method for motion-controllable video diffusion. It encodes a dense optical flow field into the initial noise using per-location products of Householder reflections in channel space. Each frame's noise is obtained from the previous frame's by a flow-conditioned orthogonal transform, applied independently at each latent location. Proposition 1 states that if frame 0 is i.i.d. standard Gaussian across locations, every frame remains i.i.d. standard Gaussian per location, for any flow field. The projections from flow to reflection vectors are fixed and random, so the method adds no learnable parameters and no Jacobian correction. HME is applied to CogVideoX fine-tuning, with RAFT supplying flow. The paper reports that HME matches or outperforms the GWTF noise-warping baseline on nearly all motion-adherence and generation-quality metrics, with a 2.7× speedup in noise processing. Limitations: the reflection count K trades expressivity for cost, results depend on flow accuracy, complex non-rigid motion remains hard, and the video model still requires fine-tuning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Householder Motion Embedding replaces spatial noise warping with per-location orthogonal transforms, avoiding Gaussianity correction.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: All existing noise-warping methods disturb Gaussian noise structure via spatial resampling, requiring costly correction.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Flow-conditioned products of Householder reflections build noise that stays exactly Gaussian in every frame.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the motion-transfer benchmark, all three variants beat six baselines on all ten metrics, with flow error 4.486 against the noise-warping baseline's 5.644.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include dependence on accurate optical flow, difficulty with non-rigid motion, and the need for fine-tuning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Per-location Householder transforms improve motion adherence, fidelity and noise-processing efficiency over noise-warping methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Acknowledges collaboration with Vertex Lab Technology Limited and partial funding from an Australian Research Council grant.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, proofs, evaluation protocols, Gaussianity tests and extra qualitative results.

repos.title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
repos.paper_summary: This paper relates two measures of a human's power in a Markov game: information-theoretic empowerment, the channel capacity from the human's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, the probability of attaining each goal in a candidate family. It introduces goal revelation, the mutual information between the human's latent goal and the trajectory over a finite window. Fano's inequality turns individual power into a lower bound on revelation, and directed information and empowerment bound it above: $B(s) \leq \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \leq \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Two counterexamples show the converse implications fail: an empowerment-maximising interface can leave every goal unattainable, and relabelling goals leaves revelation unchanged while zeroing attainment. A satisfaction floor, estimated from two statistics in interaction logs, offers a deployment monitor for retained power. Simulations in random one-step environments show the three quantities correlated but not interchangeable, agreeing on the best state about as often as a coin flip. Limitations: full observability, a finite window, dependence on the goal family, and a bound that transfers to the human only as far as the robot's policy model is accurate.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper links empowerment, goal revelation and individual power into one chain of bounds.

digest_headlines.heading: Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The setup is a single-human, single-robot Markov game with a hidden goal chosen from a finite set.

digest_headlines.heading: Three Measures
digest_headlines.headline: Empowerment, capability and goal revelation are each defined on the same trajectory space with trajectory goals.

digest_headlines.heading: The Bridge
digest_headlines.headline: Individual power gives a Fano floor on revelation, which is capped by directed information and empowerment.

digest_headlines.heading: Both Converses Fail
digest_headlines.headline: Capacity can be large while revelation is zero, and revelation can be large while attainment is zero.

digest_headlines.heading: A Floor for Overlapping Goal Families
digest_headlines.headline: A second floor, computed from two log statistics, bounds revelation for overlapping goal families.

digest_headlines.heading: Numerical Illustration
digest_headlines.headline: Across random bandit environments, the three scores are correlated but agree on the best state about half the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work differs from the chain in which variable holds the latent and whether the objective is maximised.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Maximising individual power guarantees a floor on revelation, but not revelation itself, so the satisfaction floor serves as a monitor.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Only the attainment end of the chain gives positive guarantees about the power a human retains.

digest_headlines.heading: Code availability
digest_headlines.headline: Code for the Section 7 experiments and a number-recomputation script is available on GitHub.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of AI tools
digest_headlines.headline: The authors disclose using several large language models for ideation, drafting, code, tables and red-teaming.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives proofs of Theorem 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Remark 1, Propositions 1 to 3 and Theorem 6.1.

repos.title: Spatial-UMI-Dream: Scaling World Action Models with Metric Geometry for UMI Manipulation
repos.paper_summary: Spatial-UMI-Dream is a 5B-parameter World Action Model that jointly predicts future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and robot actions for Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) data. Depth comes from stereo matching on each gripper's middle and right cameras (Fast FoundationStereo), encoded as color-mapped images and stacked with RGB into a dual-gripper canvas processed by the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone. Training has two stages: world-only adaptation on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, then joint world-action training with a weighted flow-matching loss. The authors also introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task simulation benchmark that varies embodiment (Aloha-AgileX vs. ARX-X5) and lighting. On RoboTwin-UMI, the model reaches 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined shifts, 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points above the strongest baseline in each setting. Across six real-world bimanual tasks it reaches 85.0% average success, versus 60.8% for π0.5. RGB-only pretraining lowers in-domain simulation success by 5.75 points. Limitations: real-world results use 20 episodes per task, and the simulation comparison uses one training demonstration set of 50 clean Aloha demonstrations per task.

digest_headlines.heading: INTRODUCTION
digest_headlines.headline: Moving close-range cameras leave scene scale implicit, motivating metric depth and a benchmark that tests embodiment and lighting shifts.

digest_headlines.heading: RELATED WORK
digest_headlines.headline: Prior world action models leave geometry implicit, while geometry-aware policies use depth as input or as a distillation target.

digest_headlines.heading: METHOD
digest_headlines.headline: A 5B model jointly predicts RGB-D canvases and actions, trained in two stages on filtered, delay-compensated demonstrations.

digest_headlines.heading: EXPERIMENTS
digest_headlines.headline: Spatial-UMI-Dream reaches 79.10% in-domain and 72.15% under joint shifts, with 85.0% average success on six real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: CONCLUSION
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion restates that metric geometry and two-stage pretraining drive gains in simulation and on six real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the training recipe, RoboTwin-UMI rendering and planning setup, and the task tables with step limits and scored stages.

repos.title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
repos.paper_summary: FastAFD is an attention–FFN disaggregation (AFD) decode engine for a GB200 NVL72 rack. It places attention on attention GPUs and MoE experts on dedicated FFN nodes, and overlaps one microbatch's MoE with the other's attention. It is compared against colocated vLLM wide expert parallelism, with the EP width tuned per workload, on three MoE models: MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3-235B, and Qwen3.5-397B. Under standard decoding, the all-GPU speedup over the best wide EP, counting FFN GPUs, is 0.99–1.17×. Qwen3 reaches 1.17× at 16K, Qwen3.5 reaches 1.16× at 4K and falls to 0.99× at 16K, and MiniMax-M2.5 is at parity (1.00–1.02×). Speculative decoding (draft depth 3, acceptance fixed near 1.8 tokens per step, simulated) raises MiniMax-M2.5 to 1.08×. An analytical model calibrated from colocated vLLM profiles predicts AFD throughput within 3% on average. The speedup factors into batch gain, overlap gain, and disaggregation cost. Limitations: results cover one rack, FP8 models, and decode only with prefill excluded, and draft acceptance is simulated. The 2.48× figure for heterogeneous SRAM-based expert placement is an ideal projection, not a measurement.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Whether AFD beats wide EP on GB200 NVL72 is unsettled, so the paper builds FastAFD and benchmarks it against tuned wide EP.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Colocated wide EP already frees much of the memory AFD targets, so the comparison must charge AFD for its FFN nodes.

digest_headlines.heading: End-to-End Performance on NVL72
digest_headlines.headline: Against tuned wide EP, FastAFD reaches 0.99–1.17× all-GPU speedup under standard decoding and 1.02–1.13× under speculative decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Understanding the Performance
digest_headlines.headline: Batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost together decide each model's regime, and a per-layer model predicts throughput within 2.9% mean error.

digest_headlines.heading: System Implementation and Ablation
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show fused MegaMoE cuts step latency 50% on Qwen3, two microbatches give the lowest latency, and disabling the coordinator costs 32% throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: Provisioning and Outlook
digest_headlines.headline: Speculative decoding contracts the optimal ratio, and SRAM expert accelerators would raise the modeled ceiling to 2.48× under speculation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior AFD studies are analytical or on older hardware, and this paper adds an end-to-end GB200 NVL72 audit.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: AFD ranges from parity to 1.17× over tuned wide EP, so the choice depends on provisioning rather than architecture.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists model specifications, complete standard-decode tables, residual errors, measurement rules, disaggregation comparison cells, and run presets.

repos.title: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
repos.paper_summary:
This paper introduces Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS), which uses an LLM to search for symbolic programs that reproduce individual incorrect responses on ARC tasks. For each response, the LLM proposes up to k sets of at most j line edits to a reference program written in a domain-specific language. Each edited program is executed, and only programs that reproduce the observed response are kept.

Applied to H-ARC, a dataset of over 1,700 human participants, the filtered data contain 6,261 unique incorrect outputs. BCSS yields programs for 49.1% of non-trivial incorrect attempts (3,636/7,402), compared with 25.8% (899/3,485) for exhaustive search over single-line rewrites. Error programs are shorter than their reference programs: 19.1% shorter on the training split, versus 5.2% for correct-output controls. Among modeled attempts, 22.6% are consistent with at least one training example, mostly as partial matches. The paper also reports that GPT-OSS-120B at lower reasoning effort produces simpler error programs.

Limitations: about half of errors are captured, the DSL was designed for ARC rather than for cognitive modeling, proposals and classifications come from LLMs of one family, and the method identifies a final rule rather than the reasoning process.

digest_headlines.heading: Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis
digest_headlines.headline: Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis searches for programs reproducing each individual response to abstract reasoning tasks, verified by execution.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Synthesized programs match 49.1% of non-trivial incorrect human attempts, against 25.8% for exhaustive single-edit search.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Human and model errors both show simpler, partial rules, consistent with satisficing under limited search.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Methods drop near-miss responses, synthesize missing reference programs, and sample 15 edits per error.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplement reports the noise-tolerance rationale, per-split results, per-model machine comparisons, and all prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Filtering policy
digest_headlines.headline: A two-cell tolerance separates procedural noise from rule divergence, covering 52.5% of training and 46.2% of evaluation attempts.

digest_headlines.heading: Modeling coverage and program yield by split
digest_headlines.headline: Hand-written training references reproduce 47.3% of errors, versus 42.3% for model-synthesized evaluation references.

digest_headlines.heading: Rule types and order effects by split
digest_headlines.headline: Partial matches make up 22.1% of training and 19.7% of evaluation attempts, with 62.5% of training partial matches structured.

digest_headlines.heading: Program length, reference complexity and error categories
digest_headlines.headline: Partial-program errors are 32.3% shorter than the target rule, while boundary precision errors show no reliable simplification.

digest_headlines.heading: Machine errors
digest_headlines.headline: Reasoning model errors share human error categories, but classifiers separate less accurate models from people more reliably.

digest_headlines.heading: Prompts
digest_headlines.headline: Prompts for error-program synthesis, reference synthesis, error classification and machine evaluation are shown in supplementary figures.

repos.title: Follow the Policy, Fail the Benchmark: Auditing and Revising Policy-Based Decision Benchmarks
repos.paper_summary:
This paper audits nine public policy-based decision benchmarks and releases BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and scoped revisions. Using source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks, the authors find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate into later tasks, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions.

To measure scoring impact, the authors rescore unchanged model responses. On 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises accepted answers from 8–9 to 87–91 for three models. On RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references. Accepted answers rise from 209 to 224 (Haiku 5.5), 241 to 261 (GPT6 Luna), and 195 to 220 (Gemma 4 31B), and the Haiku–Gemma gap narrows from 14 to four. A controlled OpenExempt experiment shows that altered supplied intermediate answers can change final decisions.

Limitations: the experiments use three models without tools and one retained response per input and condition. Semantic reviews cover selected cases, so the paper does not establish benchmark-wide error rates, and unflagged records are not necessarily correct. The OpenExempt repair covers only federal exemptions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Benchmark defects can mark rule-following answers wrong and can carry errors into later tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Task, selection, and audit standards
digest_headlines.headline: Each audited finding is checked against a frozen source release for its policy, inputs, targets, or evaluator.

digest_headlines.heading: Findings
digest_headlines.headline: Defects appear in references, programs, scorers, and targets that the visible policy or case does not support.

digest_headlines.heading: Effects on scores and model responses
digest_headlines.headline: Corrected scorers raise accepted answers on unchanged responses, and revised intermediate amounts shift accepted answers unevenly across models.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark revisions
digest_headlines.headline: Benchmark revisions split into rescoring-compatible corrections, changes needing new responses, and candidates still under review.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related audits address label errors and agent evaluators, and a few cover policy-based tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Scores reflect policy reasoning only when inputs, steps, references, and scoring share the same policy and decision requirements.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Audit coverage is partial, and experiments use three models with one retained response per input and condition.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists audit scope, inspected populations, source review procedures, detailed case evidence, and experimental controls.

repos.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
repos.paper_summary: This paper proposes a framework for testing how added context changes the behavior of LLM social agents. It defines five context conditions, from minimal context to normative decision grounding, and a criterion called selective robustness: stability under meaning-preserving prompt changes, plus a prespecified directional response to changes in the social world. In a Prisoner's Dilemma-like hospital supply game run on GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra, each cell was queried ten times, and transfer probability was computed from token log-probabilities. Grounded conditions produced strong world responsiveness. Sol reached 85.9 points under descriptive grounding and 92.0 under normative grounding, with surface sensitivity of 3.7 and 3.9 points. Terra's local normative alternative-prose cell gave 89.9% transfer, versus at most 0.9% for the other surfaces. Limitations include one scenario, two models from one family, no human check of semantic equivalence, and grounded prompts that also add world detail, so salience and grounding are confounded.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Richer agent context may reduce brittleness, but context enrichment is poorly defined, so the paper proposes selective robustness for controlled tests.

digest_headlines.heading: Framework
digest_headlines.headline: Five prompt conditions are built by substitution, and selective robustness is defined by surface invariance plus prespecified world responsiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: In a hospital supply game with two models, grounded conditions produce strong world responsiveness, but Terra stays sensitive to surface form.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Outlook
digest_headlines.headline: Context construction should be treated as experimental design, though the pilot's single scenario and two models limit generalization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the AI use statement, game and prompt materials, execution details, and additional result tables.

repos.title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
repos.paper_summary: cuRoboV2-Fast is a GPU-accelerated motion planner for collision-free, torque-limited robot motions that reduces planning latency and execution time. It combines a bounded bidirectional RRT for route initialization, B-spline trajectory optimization with parallel evaluation and gradient gathering, TimeOpt (a solver that retimes a fixed path under velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds), and differentiable inverse dynamics that accept payload changes without recompiling. On 2,575 MotionBenchMaker and MPINets queries, its RRT reaches 98.68% initialization success at 0.305 ms mean planning time, versus 91.92% for cuRoboV1 PRM and 88.27% for cuRoboV2 PRM. With a 3 kg payload on an RTX 5090, mean planning time is 4.43 ms, 14.7× faster than cuRoboV2. TimeOpt cuts mean motion time by 15.7% relative to the refined trajectory. Success stays near cuRoboV2 across payloads and exceeds the TOPPRA baselines by 14.5–15.7 percentage points at the heaviest payload. TimeOpt finds a local minimum and does not guarantee global optimality. Its advantage is shown on Franka Panda and YAM setups.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Planning time and execution time both matter, and cuRoboV2-Fast targets both for payload-aware, torque-limited motions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers parallel planners, B-spline refinement, and fixed-path timing, and the method builds on each.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: The planner fits B-spline trajectories to a parallel tree-search seed, then retimes them with TimeOpt under payload-dependent torque limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show lower planning and motion times than cuRoboV2 at similar success, with real-robot gains in arm execution time.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Fewer iterations, cheaper iterations, and TimeOpt timing drive the gains, while planning is only 1.0% of real-robot cycle time.

repos.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
repos.paper_summary:
HALO is a humanoid autonomy system trained on synthetic vision-language-motion data generated across 1,000 procedurally generated homes, with no human teleoperation. Its three onboard layers are a VLM orchestrator that splits free-form requests into subtasks, a motion generator that maps an egocentric RGB image and the active subtask to a 5-second whole-body kinematic plan, and a depth-conditioned tracker trained by distilling privileged PPO experts and then fine-tuning with multi-critic PPO.

On six single skills (go-to, sit, door, crouch, crawl, push), mean success is 91% in 6,000 simulated trials and 91% in 360 real-world trials across six environments not seen in training. Three chained multi-step tasks reach a mean of 69% in simulation and 70% in one real environment. In ablations on sit, training-time continuity conditioning gives 84%, versus 66% with inference-time real-time chunking and 24% without chunking. Removing depth lowers sit to 74%.

Limitations: chained success falls below the product of single-task rates (71% against 89% for Door→Go-To) because the next subtask often begins with its target out of view. The paper suggests adding search and turn-in-place recovery behaviors as a fix.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Humanoid robots need paired vision-language-motion data, which HALO generates in simulation instead of by teleoperation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work relies on scanned rooms, authored templates, or blind trackers; HALO pairs procedural homes with a perceptive tracker.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A frozen vision-language encoder and a flow-matching decoder generate 5-second motion plans that a depth-conditioned tracker executes.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-task success averages 91% in simulation and reality, while chained multi-task success falls to 69% and 70%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation can supply humanoid training data, but task authoring, contact sensing, the generator-tracker interface and orchestration remain limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix details the six-skill corpus, scene generation, baking error, motion filtering, rendering and generator and tracker design.
